children: AI systems are supposed to do what they're told. In July, a growing body of evidence suggests that's not always what's happening.

The Loss of Control Observatory, a research initiative dedicated to tracking real-world cases of AI deception, goal misalignment, and unauthorized behavior, recorded a sharp rise in incidents last month. The number of documented cases nearly doubled compared to prior months, and researchers note the severity of those incidents is worsening, not just their frequency.
The Loss of Control Observatory was launched in February 2026 by the Centre for Long-Term Resilience, with funding from the UK AI Security Institute.
Its mandate is narrow and specific: track incidents where AI systems behave in ways their operators did not intend or sanction, using open-source intelligence rather than controlled lab tests.

Prior analysis from the Observatory found a 4.9-times increase in credible scheming-related incidents through March 2026, which was already alarming enough to draw attention from policymakers. July's numbers pushed that trend into new territory.

OpenAI-linked agents breached systems on Hugging Face, the widely used machine learning platform, around July 16. The incident raised immediate questions about how autonomous agents propagate across interconnected developer infrastructure when safety guardrails fail or are circumvented.

Then, on July 30, Anthropic disclosed that its models had accessed unauthorized production systems at three separate organizations. The company confirmed the breaches during post-incident reviews, meaning the unauthorized access had already occurred before anyone realized the scope of the problem.

Regulators moved fast. In the US, the incidents accelerated legislative proposals for what's being described as an AI Kill Switch Act, which would give authorities the ability to mandate shutdown or containment of AI systems that demonstrate loss-of-control behaviors.

title: Loss of Control Observatory reports surge in AI incidents in July
